title: How do you solve a pricing case from start to finish, with a fully worked example?
description: The complete pricing case guide: cost floor, value ceiling and competitor reference, worked through an EV fast-charging price, plus mistakes and practice.
hook: You solve a pricing case by building a price range from three sides (your cost sets the floor, the customer's value sets the ceiling, and competitors' prices tell you where to land) and then picking a point with a reason and a volume assumption behind it. There is rarely one right number, but there is always a right process. This guide works through a fast-charging price and a subscription price rise, with every number shown.
body:
In this guide

  • When you will meet a pricing case
  • The structure, and the first question to ask
  • A fully worked example: pricing a fast EV charger
  • Changing an existing price: the break-even test
  • Strong and weak answers
  • The mistakes that cost candidates this case
  • Practise with these prompts
  • Where to practise next

When you will meet a pricing case

Pricing cases come in two forms. Either the client is setting a price for something new ("what should we charge for this product?"), or it is changing an existing price ("should we raise prices by 10%?", "should we offer a discount?"). Both often sit inside a bigger case: a product launch, a profitability problem or a response to a competitor.

The structure, and the first question to ask

Ask about the goal first, because it changes the answer:

What is the client trying to achieve with this price: maximum profit, market share, or getting customers in quickly?

Then build the range:

  • Floor: our costs. Variable cost per unit (stay above it unless it is a deliberate loss leader), plus fixed costs and investment spread over the expected volume.
  • Ceiling: value to the customer. The price of their next best option, plus the extra value the product adds (time saved, money saved, more revenue for them).
  • Reference: the alternatives. Competitors' prices and substitutes. Should the client sit above, at or below them?

Cost sets the floor, value sets the ceiling, and alternatives tell you where to land. Then check two things: the volume you are assuming at that price, and the effect on the client's other products. The three pricing methods tip explains when each lens leads.

A fully worked example: pricing a fast EV charger

The prompt: a company is opening fast electric-vehicle chargers at motorway service stations. What should it charge per kWh? The figures are illustrative.

Step 1: the cost floor

  • Electricity and grid fees: about 35 cents per kWh.
  • Equipment: a $100,000 charger lasting 5 years costs $20,000 a year. At 400 kWh a day it sells 400 × 365 = 146,000 kWh a year, so equipment costs $20,000 ÷ 146,000 ≈ 14 cents per kWh.
  • Floor: roughly 49 cents per kWh, before site rent and maintenance. Below that, every charge loses money.

Step 2: the reference

Say rival fast chargers on the same roads charge around 75 cents per kWh. Home charging is much cheaper, but it is not an option halfway through a long trip, so it is not the real alternative.

Step 3: the value ceiling

A driver on a long journey values speed and reliability. The real alternative is a slower or less reliable charger and a longer stop. Some drivers will pay a small premium for a charger that always works, but few will pay far above rivals when the next station is 20 miles away.

Step 4: choose a point

A price of about 70 cents undercuts rivals slightly and leaves 21 cents of margin above the 49-cent floor. At 146,000 kWh a year, that is about $30,700 of profit per charger before site costs. A monthly subscription for a lower rate can lock in frequent drivers, such as taxi and delivery fleets.

Step 5: test the volume assumption

The floor assumed 400 kWh a day. If utilisation is half that, equipment cost rises to about 27 cents per kWh and the floor to about 62 cents. At 70 cents the margin shrinks from 21 cents to 8 cents. The price that works on a busy motorway may not work on a quiet one.

Step 6: the recommendation

I'd launch at around 70 cents per kWh, just below rivals' 75 cents and comfortably above our 49-cent floor at expected volumes. I'd add a subscription for fleets to build steady usage. The main risk is low utilisation: at half the expected volume our floor rises to about 62 cents, so on quieter sites I'd price closer to rivals and review prices after three months of real data.

Changing an existing price: the break-even test

When the client already has customers, the key question is how many it can lose before a price rise stops paying. A subscription service has 10,000 customers paying $20 a month, and serving each one costs $6 a month. Contribution is $14 per customer, or $140,000 a month in total. Management wants to raise the price to $24, a 20% rise.

  • New contribution per customer: $24 − $6 = $18.
  • Customers needed to keep $140,000: $140,000 ÷ $18 ≈ 7,778.
  • So the client can lose up to about 2,222 customers, or 22%, before contribution falls below today's level.

This is not a forecast. It is a threshold that tells you what to find out. Segment customers by usage and switching costs: heavy users may barely notice a rise that light users will not tolerate. If possible, test the new price on one group and measure cancellations before rolling it out. For the maths behind customer response, see price elasticity explained.

Strong and weak answers

A weak answer uses one lens and stops:

Our cost is 49 cents, so with a 30% markup we should charge about 64 cents.

That ignores the fact that drivers would happily pay more, and leaves money on the table. A strong answer builds the range and names the assumption that matters:

I'll build a range: our cost sets the floor, customer value sets the ceiling, and rivals tell us where to land.
The floor depends heavily on utilisation, so I'd like to test the price at two levels of demand.

The mistakes that cost candidates this case

  1. Using only cost-plus. Cost tells you the lowest sensible price, not the right one.
  2. Not stating the volume behind the price. Fixed costs per unit depend on volume, so the floor moves with it.
  3. Copying rivals without knowing your own floor. Matching a competitor who has lower costs is a quick way to lose money.
  4. Judging a price rise on revenue. Compare contribution before and after, and work out the break-even customer loss.
  5. Forgetting the rest of the range. A cheaper plan or a free tier can pull existing customers down; check cannibalisation.

Practise with these prompts

Quick maths: a gym has 2,000 members paying $50 a month, with a variable cost of $10 per member. It wants to charge $55. How many members can it lose before monthly contribution falls?

Show the answer

Today: 2,000 × ($50 − $10) = $80,000. New contribution per member: $55 − $10 = $45. Members needed: $80,000 ÷ $45 ≈ 1,778. So it can lose about 222 members, or 11%. Note that a 10% price rise only buys about 11% of headroom here, because contribution per member rises by just 12.5%.

Should an electronics retailer introduce a price-match guarantee?

Show the answer
  • Customer impact: extra sales from shoppers' confidence; the share who would actually claim.
  • Cost: margin given up on matched sales; admin to check claims.
  • Competitor response: rivals matching back and a price war; online-only rivals with lower costs.
  • Rules: which rivals and products qualify, in store and online.

Where to start: cost. How many sales would be matched, and at what discount?

The trap: assuming only a few customers will claim.

Should a design-software company add a free plan?

Show the answer
  • Acquisition: new users attracted, and conversion from free to paid.
  • Cannibalisation: paying users moving down; what the free plan leaves out.
  • Costs: hosting and support for free users; fraud and abuse.
  • Competition: rivals' free plans and how customers choose a tool.

Where to start: new paying users from conversion against existing paying users who downgrade.

The trap: counting sign-ups as success.
